# Dynamic regulation of 5-formylcytidine on tRNA

**Authors:** Xuemeng Sun; Ralph E. Kleiner

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544

## Abstract

Post-transcriptional modifications on RNA play an important role in biological processes, but we lack an understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the function of many modifications. Here we characterize the distribution and dynamic regulation of 5-formylcytidine (f5C), a modification primarily found on tRNAs, across different cell lines, mouse tissues, and in response to environmental stress. We identify perturbation in bulk f5C levels using nucleoside LC-MS and quantify individual modification stoichiometry at the wobble base of mt-tRNA-Met and tRNA-Leu-CAA using nucleotide resolution f5C sequencing technology. Our studies show that f5C modifications on tRNAs are dynamic, and responsive to fluctuations in cellular iron levels and O2 concentration. Further, we show using a translation reporter assay that decoding of Leu UUA codons is impaired in cells lacking f5C, implicating f5C(m)34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA in wobble decoding. Together, our work illuminates dynamic epitranscriptomic mechanisms regulating protein translation in response to environment.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

RNA modifications are important post-transcriptional regulators of RNA function. More than 170 modifications have been identified on various RNA species, including ribosomal RNA (rRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and messenger RNA (mRNA)1, and the greatest number and diversity of these modifications are found on tRNAs. The study of tRNA modifications dates back to seminal work in tRNA biochemistry by Holley et al.2 and others, but there still remain major gaps regarding the distribution, dynamics, and function of tRNA modifications in many organisms.

Whereas many tRNA modifications are broadly conserved throughout evolution, others have more specialized distribution. One such modification, 5-formylcytidine (f5C), was initially discovered at the wobble position (C34) of mitochondrial (mt) tRNA-Met from bovine liver3. Subsequently, the presence of f5C34 was confirmed in mt-tRNA-Met across diverse species, including worm, fruit fly4, frog, rat and human5,6, but not in budding yeast7. The leading hypothesis for the biochemical function of the C5 formyl group is in stabilizing f5C-A base pairing8, which enables f5C34-modified mt-tRNA-Met to decode AUA and AUG codons in the mitochondrial genetic code9–12. Consistent with this role, cells lacking f5C34 on mt-tRNA Met, generated through depletion of the writer enzymes NSUN3 or ALKBH1 (Figure 1A), display mitochondrial translation defects and corresponding mitochondrial dysfunction5,6,13–15. Additionally, f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met plays an important role during differentiation16 and is proposed to facilitate cancer cell metastasis17. Another f5C modification identified in multiple independent studies resides at C34 of the nuclear-encoded tRNA-Leu-CAA14,18,19. ALKBH1 is required for f5C34 modification on both mt-tRNA-Met and tRNA-Leu-CAA14,15,18,19, however the initial methylation to m5C on tRNA-Leu-CAA is catalyzed by NOP2/Sun RNA Methyltransferase 2 (NSUN2)14, rather than NSUN3 (Figure 1A). In contrast to f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met, the function of f5C34 modification on tRNA-Leu-CAA in mammals is largely unknown. Further, the dynamic regulation and tissue distribution of both major f5C sites on tRNA have been poorly characterized. As both sites depend upon ALKBH1 activity, their levels may be affected by fluctuations in cellular concentrations of Fe (II), α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), or O2, which are all required ALKBH1 co-factors; alternatively, modulation could occur at the initial methylation step by NSUN2/3.

Recently, our group developed RNA-mediated activity-based protein profiling (RNABPP)18,20,21, a reactivity-based method to profile RNA-modifying enzymes and investigate their substrates. We used this strategy together with the 5-ethynylcytidine (5-EC) nucleoside probe to identify human enzymes performing m5C oxidation chemistry and to map their substrates18. We found that ALKBH1 was the primary 5-EC reactive protein in human cells and further showed with genetic knockout that ALKBH1 is responsible for installing the majority of f5C and 5-hydroxymethylcytidine (hm5C) modifications in HEK293T cells. In human cells, f5C is highly enriched in the small RNA fraction (<200nt)18 and our mapping studies with ALKBH1 individual-nucleotide resolution crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (iCLIP) and transcriptome-wide aldehyde-reactive probe (ARP)-sequencing identified mt-tRNA-Met and tRNA-Leu-CAA as the primary ALKBH1 m5C oxidation substrates18. A recent report also identified f5C sites on chromatin-associated RNA in HeLa and mESCs19. Using pyridine borane-based nucleotide resolution sequencing, we quantified f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met and on tRNA-Leu-CAA, showing that modifications levels on mt-tRNA-Met were near 100%, whereas tRNA-Leu-CAA exhibited only ~20% modification. Sub-stoichiometric modification levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA suggest that this site may be dynamically regulated, however it is unknown what factors can modulate cellular RNA f5C levels.

Here, we investigate the distribution and regulation of f5C levels across a variety of mouse tissues and human cell lines. We quantify bulk f5C modification levels using nucleoside LC-QQQ-MS and measure individual modification site-stoichiometry using targeted pyridine borane-based sequencing. Further, we study the responsiveness of different f5C modification sites to diverse stress conditions, encompassing oxidative stress, iron deprivation and hypoxia stress. Finally, we show that f5C modifications on tRNA-Leu-CAA are involved in the translation of UUA-rich reporter transcripts. Together, our study sheds light on the intricate landscape of f5C modification across diverse biological contexts, highlighting its dynamic responsiveness to stress stimuli and its potential role in modulating protein expression, thus providing valuable insights into regulatory mechanisms mediated by tRNA modifications.

## RESULTS

### f5C and hm5C levels vary among mammalian cell lines

We first sought to determine the prevalence of f5C in a variety of established human cell lines (HEK293T, MDA-MB-231, HeLa and A549) as well as in mouse tissues (Figure 1B). We used nucleoside LC-QQQ-MS analysis (Supplementary Figure 1, Supplementary Table 1) to quantify f5C in total RNA and found that HEK293T, HeLa, and MDA-MB-231 cell lines exhibited similar f5C levels (approximately 10 ppm), while A549 cells demonstrated a slightly higher f5C/C ratio of 15.5 ± 0.7 ppm (mean ± standard deviation, same below) (Figure 1C, Supplementary Figure 2). Given that known f5C sites primarily exist on tRNAs18, we further isolated the small RNA fraction (<200 nt) and conducted quantitative analysis of f5C and hm5C levels using LC-QQQ-MS. Interestingly, hm5C concentration was elevated in HEK293T (25.4 ± 3.2 ppm) and MDA-MB-231 (26.7 ± 0.4 ppm) as compared to HeLa and A549 (Figure 1D, Supplementary Figure 2). MDA-MB-231 cells (16.3 ± 1.3 ppm) exhibited lower f5C levels as compared to the other cell lines (Figure 1E, Supplementary Figure 2). 5-methylcytidine (m5C) abundance was comparable across all cell lines in the small RNA fraction (Supplementary Figure 3).

As ALKBH1 is required for f5C modification on RNA14,15,18,19, we studied the contributions from ALKBH1 to f5C and hm5C levels in cultured cells. We generated ALKBH1 KO A549 and HeLa cells using CRISPR/Cas918,22. In A549, we found 65% depletion of hm5C and 94% depletion of f5C upon ALKBH1 KO, (Supplementary Figures 4A and 4B), similar to what we reported previously in HEK293T cells18. In HeLa cells, ALKBH1 KO resulted in near complete loss of f5C, with little effect on hm5C (Supplementary Figures 4C and 4D). Taken together, our results confirm that f5C modification in immortalized human cell lines depends almost exclusively upon ALKBH1, whereas the contribution of ALKBH1 to hm5C levels is more cell-type specific. Prior work including our own has shown that TET enzymes (primarily TET2) can install hm5C on RNA18,23–27, therefore ALKBH1-independent hm5C sites in HEK293T and A549 cell lines may be installed by TET proteins, whereas in HeLa cells ALKBH1 catalyzes the majority of hm5C formation. In addition, f5C and hm5C levels vary by ~1.5–3 fold across cultured human cell lines.

### LC-MS analysis of RNA modifications in mouse tissues

Next, we extended our LC-QQQ-MS analysis to mouse tissue samples, where we observed more pronounced variations compared to immortalized human cell lines (Figures 1F, Supplementary Figure 5). Notably, the abundance of f5C was highest in the heart (244 ± 38.9 ppm), which is >10–20-fold higher than we measured in cultured human cells. Intermediate f5C levels (45–65 ppm) were detected in the kidney, brain, and brown adipose tissue (BAT). Additionally, analysis of two types of skeletal muscles revealed that f5C levels in the diaphragm (152 ± 15.1 ppm) were 2–3 times higher than in the quad (62.7 ± 30.1 ppm). Spleen, liver, lung and small intestine contained lower f5C levels (between 13–20 ppm), comparable to those we found in cultured human cells, and consistent with prior work28. Since ALKBH1 is primarily localized in mitochondria in cultured cells29, we plotted f5C levels in different mouse tissues against previously measured cytochrome c levels (a metric for mitochondrial quantity)30 (Figure 1G). Our analysis shows a strong positive correlation between f5C levels and mitochondrial quantity per tissue (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.86). Indeed, previous reports have shown that the heart is highly enriched in mitochondria30–32 with a tissue mitochondrial volume density of 20–30% in small mammals33. Given the correlation between f5C abundance and mitochondrial quantity across various tissues, we attribute elevated f5C levels primarily to f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met15,18.

Using our LC-MS platform, we also measured levels of hm5C, dihydrouridine (D), m5C, N1-methyladenosine (m1A), and N6-isopentenyladenosine (i6A), which are primarily found on tRNA, and N6-methyladenosine (m6A), which is primarily found on mRNA and rRNA. None of these modifications varied as dramatically as f5C in abundance, but we found that tRNA-specific modifications (i.e. D, m5C, m1A, i6A) have 2–3-fold higher abundance in diaphragm, quad and heart as compared to other tissues (Supplementary Figures 6 and 7), consistent with a previous study showing higher m5C and m1A in heart than other tissues34. The enrichment of tRNA-specific modifications in skeletal muscles (diaphragm, quad) and heart is likely caused by higher tRNA levels in these tissues, given a previous study discovering enrichment of mt-tRNAs in heart and skeletal muscles compared to liver35. On the other hand, the mRNA/rRNA-specific modification m6A is distributed more evenly across different tissues, with slight enrichment in the brain (Supplementary Figure 6F).

### Nucleotide resolution quantification of major f5C sites

To investigate the relationship between bulk f5C levels in different cell lines and tissues and specific f5C modifications, we employed the pyridine borane (pyBH3) sequencing method, which generates C-to-T reverse transcription (RT) misincorporation events at f5C modification sites and provides a quantitative measure of modification levels in RNA18,36,37 (Figure 2A). We focused on modifications at the wobble base (position 34) of tRNA-Leu-CAA and mt-tRNA-Met (Figure 2B), as our group and others have identified these two positions as major f5C sites in the mammalian transcriptome14,18,19. First, we analyzed levels of f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met in cultured human cells and mouse tissues. Following pyBH3 treatment, we observed high levels of C-to-T conversion ranging from 83–90% across four cultured human cell lines (HEK293T, MDA-MB-231, HeLa, and A549) and ranging from 78–85% across three mouse tissues with different bulk levels of f5C (brain, heart, and liver) (Figure 2C). In untreated samples we observed <0.5% mutation at f5C34 (Supplementary Figure 8A), consistent with previously reported RT behavior38,39. These mutation rates suggest near stoichiometric f5C modification on mt-tRNA-Met across a diverse range of mammalian cell lines and tissues, aligning with multiple prior independent reports7,19,36, and underscoring the biological importance of this modification for mitochondrial function9–12.

In contrast to the uniformly high abundance of f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met in mammalian cells, we observed significant variation in f5C34 levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA across different cultured cell lines spanning >3-fold difference in stoichiometry (MDA-MB-231: 2.3% ± 0.5%, A549: 7.5% ± 1.2%, HeLa: 2.46% ± 0.4%, and HEK293T: 7.69% ± 0.8%) (Figure 2D). We note that f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA likely exists together with f5Cm3414, and both modifications should be detected by pyBH3-mediated C-to-T conversion analysis. Although pyBH3 conversion rates are low for tRNA-Leu-CAA sites, they are still significantly higher than control samples where conversion rates are less than 0.5% (Supplementary Figure 8B). In mouse tissues, we observed even lower f5C34 levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA with modest differences across the three sampled tissues (brain: 3.1% ± 0.7%, heart: 2.7% ± 0.3%, and liver: 2.0% ± 0.6%). Despite differences in total f5C levels among these tissues (brain: 60.8 ± 26.2 ppm; heart: 244 ± 38.9 ppm; liver: 19.2 ± 1.1 ppm; as shown in Figure 1F), f5C modification levels at both tRNA-Leu-CAA and mt-tRNA-Met wobble positions are similar, suggesting that differences in bulk f5C levels likely stem from differences in mitochondrial number/size, rather than modification stoichiometry.

### Stress conditions can induce alterations in f5C levels

As numerous RNA modifications are dynamically regulated in response to stress40–42, we investigated whether f5C levels were affected by environmental stress conditions including oxidative stress, iron starvation, and nutrient deprivation. First, we used nucleoside LC-QQQ-MS to measure bulk f5C levels in small RNA extracted from HEK293T cells subjected to stress or control conditions. To deplete cellular iron levels, we incubated cells with 100 μM deferoxamine mesylate salt (DFO) for 24h and observed 55.3% to 68.7% reduction in bulk f5C levels on small RNA (Figure 3A, Supplementary Figure 9A and 10A), consistent with the important role of Fe2+ for ALKBH1 catalysis. A statistically significant, but smaller decrease was observed in total RNA f5C level (Supplementary Figure 9B). Oxidative stress induced by H2O2 treatment (500 μM for 1 hr) resulted in a 31.3% ± 9.0% decrease in f5C levels (Figure 3A, Supplementary Figure 9A and 10A). Previously, Tardu et al. also observed a decrease in f5C levels in yeast subjected to H2O2 stress43. We did not observe changes in bulk f5C levels on small RNA after serum starvation. Levels of hm5C on small RNA isolated from stressed HEK293T cells showed similar trends to f5C and decreased upon DFO or H2O2 treatment, while remaining unchanged in response to serum starvation (Figure 3B, Supplementary Figures 9C and 10B). We also monitored the levels of abundant tRNA modifications, including m5C and m1A, (substrates of ALKBH1 enzyme18,44), and D, but no significant differences were observed in either total RNA or small RNA under the stress conditions assayed (Supplementary Figures 9D and 9E). While ALKBH1 can demethylate m1A on tRNA, previous studies have shown that knockdown or knockout of ALKBH1 increases m1A levels only modestly18,44, therefore partial impairment of ALKBH1 function as a result of stress is unlikely to produce major changes in bulk levels of this abundant modification.

Since we observed the largest changes in f5C and hm5C with DFO treatment, we further subjected HEK293T cells to varying concentrations of DFO and measured corresponding f5C/hm5C levels from small RNA. Our observations revealed a dose-dependent decrease in hm5C levels as DFO was titrated from 30 μM to 120 μM, with an 82% ± 3.2% reduction at 120 μM DFO (Figure 3C, Supplementary Figures 11 and 12). Interestingly, whereas 30 μM DFO treatment reduced f5C levels by 50% ± 13.1% (Figure 3D, Supplementary Figures 11 and 12), we did not observe further decreases with 60 μM or 120 μM DFO treatment. Consistent with previous measurements, no significant difference was detected in m5C or m1A modification levels (Supplementary Figure 11B). Additionally, we found a similar trend when DFO treatment was extended to 48 h, indicating the existence of a pool of f5C-modified small RNA that remains modified upon treatment (Supplementary Figure 11C). However, m5C and m1A level also decreased during 48 h DFO treatment, indicating that prolonged iron depletion causes global tRNA stress (Supplementary Figure 11D).

To investigate site-specific changes in f5C during stress, we utilized targeted pyBH3 sequencing on tRNA-Leu-CAA and mt-tRNA-Met as described above. At f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA, C-to-T conversion decreased from 7.7% ± 0.8% to 2.2% ± 0.6% (a ~70% reduction) with 30 μM DFO but did not decrease below 2% with 60 μM or 120 μM DFO treatment (Figure 3E). On mt-tRNA-Met, f5C34 decreased in a dose-dependent manner with increasing DFO concentration (Figure 3F). However, even at the highest DFO treatment (120 μM), we observed only ~50% reduction in modification levels, whereas f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA exhibited a more substantial 71.4% decrease at a lower 30 μM DFO treatment. Taken together, our data show that iron chelation reduces bulk f5C/hm5C levels and specific f5C modification levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA and mt-tRNA-Met. Of these two major f5C sites, f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA displays greater responsiveness to DFO-mediated iron chelation; however, we could not completely reduce f5C levels on either tRNA transcript, suggesting a subpopulation of both tRNAs that is stably modified even at low Fe2+ concentration.

### f5C modifications are regulated by O2 levels

Given that enzymatic hm5C/f5C formation by ALKBH1 uses O2 as a substrate, we next investigated whether fluctuations in O2 levels would impact modification. We cultured HEK293T and A549 cells under hypoxic conditions (1% O2) and isolated small RNA for nucleoside LC-QQQ-MS analysis. When compared to control cells grown under atmospheric O2 (~20%), we observed a 24% ± 11.8% reduction in hm5C and 38% ± 6.2% decrease in f5C in HEK293T cells (Figure 4A, Supplementary Figure 13A and 14), and 28% ± 15.6% decrease in hm5C and 37% ± 14.4% reduction in f5C in A549 cells (Figure 4B, Supplementary Figure 13B and 14). Other RNA modifications that we measured such as m5C and m1A were largely unaffected by O2 concentration (Supplementary Figure 13C and 13D). This aligns with a zebrafish study that reported only modest changes in overall level of m5C and m1A in mRNA under hypoxia conditions, as measured by MeRIP-Seq45.

Using targeted pyBH3 sequencing, we also measured site-specific alterations in f5C on mt-tRNA-Met and tRNA-Leu-CAA in response to hypoxia. In HEK293T cells, we observed a 38.7% ± 10.0% decrease in f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA (Figure 4C), and in A549 a more pronounced decrease of 59.9% ± 3.0% (Figure 4D). In contrast, f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met in both HEK293T and A549 was more modestly responsive to O2 levels, with only a 16.6% ± 0.9% reduction in HEK293T cells (Figure 4E) and a 23.4% ± 0.3% reduction in A549 cells (Figure 4F). Taken together, we find that f5C34 levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA and mt-tRNA-Met are both sensitive to O2 concentration, with more dramatic changes observed on tRNA-Leu-CAA, mirroring our observations during iron deprivation.

### ALKBH1 enhances decoding of UUA codons during translation

Building upon our understanding of the function of f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met in decoding both AUG and AUA codons during mitochondrial translation9–12, we investigated whether f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA may play a similar role in decoding Leu(UUA) codons during cytosolic translation. To test this hypothesis, we utilized a codon-specific dual luciferase-based translation assay (Figure 5A). Previously, using a similar assay we demonstrated that under stress conditions, ALKBH1 KO cells exhibited a translation defect in elongation through a 5X UUA codon linker as compared to WT cells18, however no significant difference was observed under normal conditions. Therefore, to amplify translation elongation defects we extended the linker to include 15 repeats of Leu UUA or Leu UUG codons. In this system, we measured a 44% ± 6.0% decrease in translation elongation efficiency in ALKBH1 KO cells on the 15x UUA reporter compared with WT, whereas no significant difference was found using a 15x UUG construct or random linker control (Figure 5B, Supplementary Table 2). To investigate whether translation defects were related to tRNA expression levels (as opposed to enhanced f5C34 wobble pairing) we measured tRNA-Leu-CAA abundance in WT vs. ALKBH1 KO cells by Northern blot and found that levels were comparable (Supplementary Figure 15). In addition, we found that levels of the related tRNA-Leu-TAA (which should decode UUA codons) were unchanged upon ALKBH1 KO (Supplementary Figures 15C and 15D). Therefore, the observed changes in translation elongation in the dual luciferase-based assay are not likely to result from alterations in tRNA levels due to ALKBH1 KO. Finally, we studied whether changes in f5C34 levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA induced by hypoxia would result in changes in translation elongation of Leu UUA/UUG codons. We did not observe any major differences in translation efficiency between normal conditions and hypoxia conditions for either UUA or UUG codon linkers (Supplementary Figure 16, Supplementary Table 3), however protein levels for both luciferase constructs under hypoxic conditions were greatly reduced, consistent with global translation inhibition during hypoxia stress46,47. We speculate that hypoxia-induced translation inhibition may overshadow any codon-specific effects resulting from changes in tRNA wobble modification levels.

## DISCUSSION

Our study has characterized the distribution and dynamics of 5-formylcytidine (f5C) among various human cell lines and different mouse tissues, both in bulk and at specific tRNA modification sites. We find that f5C is highly enriched in tissues containing high mitochondrial quantity, consistent with the mitochondrial localization of the f5C writer, ALKBH1, and its major substrate mt-tRNA-Met. In addition, we show that f5C modification levels at the wobble positions of mt-tRNA-Met and tRNA-Leu-CAA are responsive to environmental stressors, including fluctuations in iron and O2 concentration. Utilizing a codon-specific translation assay, we show that ALKBH1 KO cells are deficient in translation of Leu UUA codons, consistent with a role for f5C(m)34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA in wobble decoding. Taken together, this work expands our understanding of the biological role of f5C modifications on tRNA, and their ability to modulate gene expression in response to environmental inputs.

RNA modifications can play a dynamic role in regulating gene expression. We observed a consistent decrease in the abundance of bulk f5C and f5C34 levels on mt-tRNA-Met and tRNA-Leu during both iron deprivation (DFO treatment) and hypoxia stress. This observation aligns with the known requirement of ALKBH1 for both Fe2+ and O2 as cofactors. Such findings are particularly relevant in the context of cellular responses to iron deficiency and low O2 environments, both of which are common in various pathophysiological conditions, including cancer, ischemic diseases, and chronic inflammation48,49. Previous reports showed that f5C in mitochondria can affect cell differentiation16 and cancer metastasis17. Therefore, we speculate that f5C tRNA modifications may play a role in the cellular response to fluctuations in O2 concentration by modulating decoding and protein translation, as O2 gradients exist during embryonic development and in the microenvironment of some stem cell48 as well as solid tumors50. Understanding how f5C levels are modulated by ALKBH1 and its cofactors provides valuable insight into the dynamic regulation of epigenetic marks and their broader implications for gene expression and cellular adaptation to stress.

We observed a more pronounced change in f5C abundance on tRNA-Leu-CAA as compared to mt-tRNA-Met under both iron deprivation and hypoxic conditions. Whereas the mechanism of f5C reduction on tRNA is uncertain (i.e. is it actively removed or diluted during tRNA turnover), for iron deprivation, this may be attributed to the reduced ability of DFO to perturb mitochondrial iron levels, as DFO lacks cell permeability51; however, the effect of hypoxia appears to be more homogeneous across different cellular compartments52,53. Since tRNA-Leu-CAA is modified at lower stoichiometry and is primarily found in the nucleus/cytoplasm whereas ALKBH1 is mitochondrial, we speculate that installation of f5C on mt-tRNA-Met is more robust across a range of co-factor concentrations – likely due to the importance of f5C34 for global mitochondrial translation9–12. Nevertheless, we do find decreased f5C34 on mt-tRNA-Met during low O2 concentration, suggesting that this modification may function as a rheostat linking environmental O2 levels to mitochondrial translation. Similarly, f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA may serve an analogous role for translation of a subset of cytosolic proteins enriched in cognate codons during hypoxia. While we did not directly measure the efficiency of Fe depletion by DFO in our system, previous studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing intracellular iron levels and inhibiting Fe(II)-dependent enzymes54–56. Given that Fe depletion could impact multiple Fe-utilizing enzymes beyond ALKBH1, we cannot rule out potential indirect effects, as the differential reduction of f5C and hm5C in ALKBH1 KO cells may involve contributions from other enzymes, including TET enzymes that have been implicated in hm5C formation on RNA18,23,26,27.

To investigate the role of f5C34 on tRNA-Leu-CAA, we used a dual luciferase-based translation assay to measure decoding of Leu UUA and UUG codons in WT and ALKBH1 KO cells. Importantly, we did not find differences in tRNA abundance of tRNA-Leu-CAA and tRNA-Leu-TAA isodecoders upon ALKBH1 KO, suggesting that the observed translational defects in ALKBH1 KO cells are related to RNA modification-dependent decoding and/or other key steps during ribosome elongation. The defect observed in translation of UUA codons in the reporter construct in ALKBH1 KO cells suggests a role for f5C in the expression of proteins enriched in UUA codon. However, it is important to note that our translation assay represents an artificial system, and confirming these effects on endogenous proteins would provide more robust evidence. Nevertheless, UUA is a rare codon in the human proteome, and proteins rich in UUA codons are typically low in abundance57. This inherent rarity makes it challenging to detect differences in endogenous protein levels. Previously, Chan et al. reported similar findings using proteomics to correlate a decrease in UUA-containing proteins with reduction in ALKBH1 expression levels58.

In summary, our findings are consistent with a model in which modulation of f5C levels on tRNA-Leu-CAA and mt-tRNA-Met due to environmental stress enables fine tuning of protein expression levels within cells. Our work motivates further study of the relationship between f5C dynamics and translational control in diverse biological systems, which may shed additional light on the mechanism and importance of gene expression regulation by tRNA modifications.
